messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am trying to compare the higher-order effects available for directed
networks in PNet with the ones in the ergm package.

What is not clear to me is whether with directed networks  the GWESP
term corresponds to the AT-C or the AT-T parameters in PNet terminology.
In other words, does the GWESP term represent higher-order transitive
closure or cyclic closure?

On the other hand, I assume that the GWDSP term with directed networks
corresponds to the A2P-T term in PNet. In other words, an higher-order
2-path parameter.

Could anyone more knowledgeable please help me?

Thanks in advance and regards,
Guido

hi guido and dave,

i've used both pnet and statnet for ERG modeling, and am pretty sure 
that GWESP corresponds to AT-T (transitive closure), while you are right

that a higher-order term for cyclic closure (or "activity closure" or 
"popularity closure") currently exists in statnet. hope this helps!

-kevin

messages.subject: [statnet_help] direct assignment of network object
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Wincent -

On 10/12/2010 07:20 AM, Wincent wrote:
> It seems that direct assignment behaves NOT in the same manner as
> 'network.copy'.  Is it a bug?

Odd -- this was working in earlier R versions, so it seems to be a 
relatively recent break.  Looks like an issue with R's deferred 
evaluation mechanism.  In particular, note that if you modify g or newg 
(e.g., by adding edges) prior to the delete.vertices call, you do not 
get this effect.  I expect that R delays the network.copy operation 
(which, BTW, is what the assignment operator does) too long, and 
delete.vertices thus gets a pointer to the original object, rather than 
to the copy (that has not yet been made).  That would be my initial 
guess, at least.

I'll put in a patch on the latest version (now on CRAN!), but in the 
interim, here is a workaround.  After you generate the new copy, you can 
force it to be evaluated by a command like

newg[1,1]<-0

or even

g[1,1]<-0

This will have no obvious effect, but will force R to evaluate the 
assignment (and hence network.copy), breaking the tie between the 
objects.  Likely, there are many other commands that would also work, 
but this is an easy option.  It works fine on my system, but let me know 
if it doesn't work for you....

Thanks!

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] interaction effects and absdiff term
messages.body_plain:
Hi Markus.

One approach is to code up a whole matrix of "interaction terms" and  
then enter this into the model as a dyadcov term.  However, depending  
on what you wish to put in the "...", there may be a simpler way:  If  
you are only using model terms that result in independence of the  
edges, then the ergm function is really just doing logistic  
regression.  Thus, you can use the ergmMPLE function to give you the  
response and predictors that may be fed into a logistic regression,  
and then you can use the usual interaction-term capability of the glm  
function.  See help(ergmMPLE) for details on this function.

Hope this helps.

Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] missing edges
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nicola,

"ergm" interprets the value of NA for an edge as meaning that information about the presence or absence of that edge is missing.

When an ERGM model is fit, ergm() uses the methods developed by the "statnet" team to find the MLE of the parameters given the observed data. This is detailed in:

"Modeling social networks from sampled data"
Mark S. Handcock and Krista J. Gile
Annals of Applied Statistics, Volume 4, Number 1 (2010), 5-25.
<http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.aoas/1273584445>

In particular, these estimates and models can be interpreted in the same way as those without missing or sampled data.

It is worthwhile noting that "latentnet" also computes estimates that adjust for missing data.

I hope this helps.

Mark

messages.subject: [statnet_help] A toy example for STATNET
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Hamid -

On 10/23/2010 11:54 PM, Hamid Ghofrani wrote:
> Dear All,
> My question is whether there is any asymptotic assumptions for ERGM?

Yes.  (A less general question might yield a less generic answer.)

> Why isn't there any example for small size graphs?

I believe you will find some such examples in the ergm man pages.

> I was trying to create a toy example, an undirected network of 10 nodes
> and created 3 triangles 123, 456, 789 ( according to node labels).
> model <- ergm(m ~
> triangle,control=control.ergm(check.degeneracy=T),maxit=50)
> Every model ended up being degenerate.
> I needed to use a small network so that I would be able to calculate the
> exact value for normalizing constant.
> The dependence structure is very simple, It has only 3 triangles and
> nothing else so What would be the cause for degeneracy?
> Is there any minimum number of nodes we need to have in STATNET package?

The pure triangle model is the textbook case of a degenerate model -- 
see Strauss's 1986 SIAM Review paper for an analysis.  Heuristically, it 
is easy to see why this is so.  Let t be the triangle count in a simple 
graph of order N, and let theta be the associated parameter.  For 
theta>0, the complete graph (K_N) is clearly of maximum probability 
(since graph probability is proportional to exp(theta*t(G)), and this 
has a unique maximum at G=K_N).  Consider the probability ratio for K_N 
versus some other graph, G', under this model.  If G' is not complete, 
it is missing at least one edge; thus, t(K_N)-t(G')>=N-2.  (This is 
because you will break N-2 triangles by removing an edge from a complete 
graph on N vertices.)  Recalling that normalizing factors cancel here, 
the ratio of graph probabilities is

Pr(G')/Pr(K_N) =  exp(theta*t(G'))/exp(theta*t(K_N))
                =  exp(theta*(t(G')-t(K_N)))
                <= exp(-theta*(N-2))

This falls exponentially fast in N -- the probability of observing any 
other graph versus the complete graph rapidly becomes very small.  This 
alone is not a proof of degeneracy, but it should suggest the nature of 
the phenomenon.  From a more pragmatic viewpoint, let us consider an 
MCMC seeking to simulate draws from this model (via a Metropolis 
algorithm with single edge updates), and ask what happens when the 
Markov chain arrives at K_N.  From the above, the probability of 
accepting any proposal (all of which involve a single edge removal) will 
be exp(-theta*(N-2)); the expected waiting time for a move away from K_N 
will then be the reciprocal of this (since the waiting time here is 
geometrically distributed), or exp(theta*(N-2)).  For the chain to move 
freely away from the complete graph, we need this to be reasonably 
small...say, exp(theta*(N-2))<=k, where k is on the order of 10 to 100. 
  That suggests that theta needs to be very small, e.g.

         N=10    N=100   N=1000
k=10    0.288   0.023   0.002
k=100   0.576   0.047   0.005

in order for the chain to mix.  Increasing theta beyond this point will 
lead the waiting times for exit from the complete graph to increase 
exponentially fast (thus effectively killing the MCMC).  Even if N=10, 
that can still ruin your life -- increase your theta from 0.288 to 1, 
and you are now waiting about 3000 iterations for a single exit. 
Increase it further from 1 to 2, and you are waiting for almost 9 
million iterations.  Further increases are clearly contraindicated for 
those with finite life spans.

I've written this somewhat extensive response because I encounter this 
question frequently, and hope that this answer may be of use to others. 
  (Also, the topic is very interesting.)  The general object lessons to 
be drawn include the following:

1. The triangle model is unsafe at any speed (per Strauss).

2. The degenerate models we tend to encounter have bad behavior that 
grows exponentially worse in the parameters.  Thus, even a small graph 
will not always save you -- there is a high-entropy region in which 
things will work, but the system freezes very quickly once one exits 
that region.  (See Handcock's 2003 chapter for a very nice example of 
how small and irregular those regions can be.)  The fact that this 
region itself often shrinks exponentially fast in N just adds additional 
excitement to the problem.

3. One can often gain an intuition for the extent of the degeneracy 
problem by examining the conditional probabilities of edge 
additions/deletions near the mode (or modes, in some cases).  This is 
not perfect, but has the virtue of mapping directly onto MCMC behavior.


One final cautionary: as my colleagues have often noted, degeneracy is 
not simply a problem of the MCMC (although the former tends to wreak 
havoc with the latter, and the latter is often used heuristically to 
identify the former).  The triangle model is still going to concentrate 
its mass on the complete graph when theta>0, and no simulation method is 
going to change that.  Finding simulation methods that let us get better 
performance for near-degenerate models is an active research area, and 
likewise there are ways that existing MCMC schemes can perform poorly on 
otherwise tolerable models (see Snijders 2002 JoSS paper for some of 
these issues); when things really don't seem to work, however, one 
should entertain the possibility that one's model may be too close to 
the degenerate limit to be salvaged by any degree of computational 
wizardry.  Techniques such as heuristic analysis of probability ratios 
(as performed above) can be helpful in determining whether this is in 
fact the case.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] BIC interpretation in Latentnet
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet users,

I am running latent space models using the package latentnet to quantify spatial networks based on animal movement. I am interested in comparing among models using model selection criteria. Based on my reading of the documentation of latentnet, it is unclear whether BIC is scaled such that 'smaller is better' or 'larger is better'. One of the examples in the latentnet manual suggests that smaller is better (on the summary.ergmm page), but on another page (the ergmm page), under BIC it cites Handcock et al. (2005). In that article (and Handcock et al. 2007), they select the model with the largest BIC. Could someone please clarify if smaller or larger BIC values are better in this package?

Also, I have been unable to find any documentation regarding the component BIC values that are provided (e.g., for latent spacing/clustering, random effects, etc.). I assume that the clustering BIC component comes from Hancock et al. (2007), but it is not clear about how this applies when G=1 and there is only latent space dimensions (and no clustering specified). Should these be used for model selection, or the overall BIC?

Thanks,

Rob Fletcher
